title: The Eight-Percent Bet
protagonist: Marcus Hale, finance director of the Harbor City Gulls (fictional baseball club)
primary_metric: pool-to-debt ratio on the first payment date (invested pool value divided by the deferred salary grown at the deferral rate); The Long Bet beats The Clean Check when the ratio is at least one

options.A: The Clean Check — pay the full salary owed today and owe the player nothing afterward
options.B: The Long Bet — defer the salary at the agent's interest rate and invest the cash under the club's policy to cover what the club will owe

The case is a genuine reinforcement of thin Calculus/Discrete/Statistics skills in a finance setting.

scenario_constructions: Marcus Hale and the Harbor City Gulls are fictional, invented for this case (corpus convention: Rosa Delgado / Fermenter, Dana Osei / The Cold Hit). The deal's terms (salary owed, interest rate, number of payments, first-payment gap, yearly payment) are modeled on a real reported 2000 deferral involving a New York baseball club; at research time these are sourced as a reported real deal and, where unverifiable, accepted as Modeling Assumptions. The case's all-January timeline is a stated simplification of the real July 1 payments.
sensitivity_note: SPEC §6 does not apply to students. A facilitator-only note on financial fraud (the real club's ownership reportedly invested with Bernard Madoff) lives in FACILITATOR.md and must never appear in student text or any student export; no living owner is named.

deliverables.text: The debt on the first payment date: the exponential expression for the unpaid salary grown at the deferral rate to the first payment date, evaluated.

The repayment schedule three ways: (a) recursive formula and a filled balance table that finds the level yearly payment; (b) the explicit formula for the balance solved for the same payment; (c) the payment stream as a sequence, the written term-by-term sum of discounted values, collapsed with the geometric-series formula. All three must agree with the contract's payment.
The pool-to-debt ratio across every historical run of the same length as the wait, as a box-and-whisker plot with median and quartiles labeled, and the share of runs with a ratio of at least one.

The same record cut into non-overlapping blocks from a start year the student chooses: each block's ratio, the mean of those ratios, how many are at least one, and why overlapping runs overstate the evidence.
What actually happened: the ratio and dollar net position for the real run beginning in the signing year, and a one-sentence verdict (bad decision or bad outcome) backed by D3 and D4.
The shortfall plan: the yearly gap payment at a student-chosen funding rate and two other rates, who covers a shortfall and who keeps a surplus, and the gap converted into roster spots.

appendices.title: The Club's Investment Policy and the Roster

balance.argument_a: The Clean Check removes all uncertainty: paying today makes the club's obligation exactly zero. The pool in The Long Bet must beat the deferral rate every year, after rebalancing, under a capped share of stocks; the historical record shows it clears the grown debt only about half the time, and when it fails the shortfall is large (figures to be research-confirmed).
balance.argument_b: The Long Bet keeps the cash working and the median historical run clears the grown debt slightly, with a larger upside than downside in dollars the club keeps; any shortfall is spread over the repayment years from a roster budget and the club keeps any surplus (figures to be research-confirmed).
balance.margin_basis: Compare the median pool-to-debt ratio at the club's policy mix against one (the sign of the net position), as a percent of the debt, once Appendix A's terms and Appendix B's return series are sourced. A is a zero-net benchmark, so the margin is the median ratio's distance from one; a stocks-only pool is a sensitivity row, not the primary comparison.

context_glossary.desc: Pay that is owed now but paid later. Here the club keeps its cash today, the unpaid salary grows at the agreed interest rate, and the club pays it back in yearly installments later.

A loan to the U.S. government that pays a fixed rate of interest twice a year until it matures. Strictly, Treasury calls a 10-year security a 'note'; this case uses the market's name, '10-year Treasury bond'.
A stock-market index that tracks about 500 large U.S. companies, weighted by their market value. Buying 'the index' means owning a small slice of all of them at once.

context_why_notes.D1: Why compare with the grown debt, not the salary: the unpaid amount earns interest while it waits, so what is owed on the first payment date is not the number in the contract's first line.
context_why_notes.D2: Why three methods: a table, a formula and a series are three views of one loan; if they disagree, one has an error. The agreement is your check.
context_why_notes.D3: Why many starting years: one run of the market is one story; the full record shows how wide the range of outcomes can be.
context_why_notes.D4: Why non-overlapping blocks: runs that share years are not independent evidence, so counting them all overstates how much we know.
context_why_notes.D5: Why look at the real run: a decision can be sound and still turn out badly, or the reverse; this separates the choice from the outcome.
context_why_notes.D6: Why a funding rate and roster spots: a shortfall is paid by someone, and turning dollars into people on a roster shows what it costs.
